lines.text: A handful of companies now run the digital world. Here is how they grew, from punched cards to pocket computers and the race for artificial intelligence.
It starts with IBM, Big Blue, which sold punched card machines, then mainframes, and for decades simply was computing.
In 1950 Steve Wozniak was born. His clever, cheap circuit designs would one day help make the personal computer practical.
Five years later came Steve Jobs, the salesman and showman who would take computers, and later phones, to the whole world.
That same year Bill Gates was born. His software would end up running most of the world's personal computers.
Tim Cook, born in 1960, would one day run Apple's factories and then the whole company after Jobs.
Jensen Huang, born in Taiwan in 1963, would co-found Nvidia, whose graphics chips now power modern AI.
And Jeff Bezos, born in 1964, would turn an online bookshop into a store and a cloud that span the globe.
In 1968 Intel was founded. It made the first microprocessor and, for decades, the chip inside most PCs.
A year later in South Korea, Samsung began making electronics. Today it is the world's largest maker of phones, memory chips and televisions.
Elon Musk, born in South Africa in 1971, would go on to PayPal, then lead Tesla and found SpaceX.
In 1975 Gates and Paul Allen founded Microsoft to write BASIC for a hobby computer. Its software would soon be on almost every desk.
A year later Jobs and Wozniak started Apple in California, a company that would one day be among the most valuable on Earth.
Its first product, the Apple I, was a bare circuit board for hobbyists. Only about two hundred were made, but it launched the company.
Then came the Apple the second, with colour graphics and room to grow. The first spreadsheet made it a business machine, and it sold for sixteen years.
In 1981 Microsoft licensed MS-DOS to IBM for its new PC. Every compatible PC booted into it for a decade, and it made Microsoft's fortune.
Microsoft also made Flight Simulator, which began as simple lines on early screens and grew into a detailed model of the whole Earth.
Apple's Lisa brought a mouse and windows on screen years ahead of rivals. It was slow and far too costly, and it flopped.
That same year came Microsoft Word. By the nineties it was the program most people used to write anything.
In 1984 Apple launched the Macintosh with a famous Super Bowl advert, bringing the mouse and the friendly screen to a mass market.
Also in 1984, Mark Zuckerberg was born. Twenty years later he would start Facebook in a Harvard dorm.
Next came Excel, Microsoft's spreadsheet, which pushed aside Lotus and became the tool every office runs on.
In 1987 Morris Chang founded TSMC in Taiwan, a company that makes chips for others. Today much of the world's technology relies on its factories.
The same year in China, Huawei was founded, and would grow into a giant of phone networks and phones.
And PowerPoint arrived, soon bought by Microsoft, to become the slide show of every meeting and classroom.
Pushed out of Apple, Jobs built NeXT, a black cube that sold poorly. Yet the first web browser was written on one, and its software lives on in today's Macs.
In 1990 Microsoft bundled Word, Excel and PowerPoint as Office, which became the standard toolkit of offices and schools worldwide.
Apple's PowerBook set the shape of the laptop, with the keyboard pushed back and room for your wrists in front. Others soon copied it.
In 1993 Jensen Huang co-founded Nvidia to make graphics chips for games. Decades later, those same chips would turn out to be what AI needs.
Apple's Newton tried to read handwriting on a screen, and was mocked for getting it wrong. Its ideas returned years later in the iPhone and iPad.
In 1995 Amazon opened as a bookshop on the web. It would grow into the store that sells nearly everything.
That summer Windows 95 launched to the Rolling Stones, bringing the Start button and taskbar that shaped Windows for decades.
Hotmail offered free email in any browser. Microsoft bought it within eighteen months, and it lives on today as Outlook.com.
Then came Google, which ranked pages by the links pointing to them. Its answers were so good that its name became a verb.
In 1998 the US government sued Microsoft for bundling its browser with Windows. A breakup was ordered, then overturned, and the case was settled.
Back at Apple, Jobs returned and launched the iMac, a colourful, see-through computer built for the internet. It pulled Apple back from the edge.
In China, Tencent was founded. It would build WeChat and the largest video game business in the world.
A year later Jack Ma founded Alibaba, which became the giant of Chinese online shopping.
Meanwhile MSN Messenger, with its nudges and winks, became where young people chatted online throughout the 2000s.
In 2001 Apple put a thousand songs in your pocket. The iPod turned Apple into a consumer electronics company.
That same year Microsoft entered gaming with the Xbox. With Halo and Xbox Live, online play on a console became normal.
Two years later the iTunes Store sold single songs for under a dollar, and persuaded people to pay for music again.
In 2003 Tesla was founded. Under Elon Musk, it would make the electric car something people actually wanted.
Skype made free calls over the internet so common that its name meant a video call, until Zoom and phone apps took over.
Google launched Gmail on April Fools' Day with a gigabyte of free space, hundreds of times more than rivals. Many thought it was a joke.
That year Facebook was born. Later renamed Meta, it came to own Instagram and WhatsApp too.
In 2005 Google Maps let anyone drag the world around and ask for directions. The paper road atlas never recovered.
YouTube arrived the same year, a place where anyone could post a video. Today it is the second most visited site in the world.
And Google Earth turned satellite photos into a globe you could spin and fly over from your desk.
Microsoft's Xbox 360 made online play and downloaded games and films part of an ordinary console.
In 2006 Amazon began renting out its computers. Amazon Web Services grew into the cloud that runs much of the internet.
Google Docs let several people write the same document at once, right in the browser.
Microsoft answered the iPod with the Zune. It arrived five years late and never came close.
Then, in 2007, Jobs unveiled the iPhone: a full web browser and a touch screen in your pocket. It became the most profitable product in history.
The next year Jobs pulled the MacBook Air out of a paper envelope on stage, setting the pattern for slim laptops.
The App Store opened that summer, letting anyone sell software to iPhone owners, and turned phones into real computers.
Google's answer was Android, built on Linux and given to phone makers for free. It became the most used operating system in the world.
In 2009 Microsoft launched Bing to take on Google. It has stayed a distant second ever since.
In 2010 the iPad made tablets popular, after years of failed attempts by others.
That same year, Kinect let Xbox players control games with their bodies and voices, no controller needed.
In 2011 came Chromebooks, cheap laptops that live on the web. They became a fixture in American schools.
Apple added iMessage, blue bubbles between Apple devices, and a big reason many people never leave the iPhone.
And Siri put a talking assistant in millions of pockets on the iPhone 4S, years before chatbots.
In 2012 Microsoft built its own computer for the first time, the Surface, a tablet whose cover was a keyboard.
Google's Chromecast, a small cheap stick, let a phone send video to any television.
The Xbox One aimed to be the box for the whole living room, but its price and early rules drew criticism, and it trailed the PlayStation.
Microsoft's voice assistant Cortana, named after a Halo character, never caught up, and was slowly retired in favour of Copilot.
In 2015 the Apple Watch turned the watch into something that counts steps and reads your heart. It became the best-selling wearable in the world.
That summer Apple Music launched, taking on Spotify for your monthly subscription.
And in San Francisco, Sam Altman, Elon Musk and others founded OpenAI. Its ChatGPT would later start the race for large language models.
Google Assistant could hold a real two-way conversation, and reached more than a billion devices before Gemini replaced it.
Apple dropped the headphone socket and sold AirPods instead. Wireless earbuds were suddenly everywhere.
Microsoft Teams arrived for office chat and meetings. When the world worked from home in 2020, its use exploded.
Google Stadia streamed big games with no console. The technology worked, but too few people signed up, and it closed.
In 2020 Apple replaced Intel with its own M1 chip. It was faster and used far less power, proving ARM could run full computers.
As the AI race heated up, Google launched Bard to answer ChatGPT, then renamed it Gemini a year later.
And in 2024 Apple released Vision Pro, a headset that blends apps with the room around you. Praised, but costly, it sold slowly.
From punched cards to thinking machines, a few companies built the world we now live in online.
